pass_a_gloss: [Cont.] under penalty (ὑπὸ δίκην); then indeed, having grieved (ἐπιστυγνάσας) at his own carelessness (ῥᾳθυμίαις), and all but crying out against (κατακεκράξεται) the strictness (ἀκριβείας) of the law, [he will cry] saying: [Rom 7:9-10a] I lived without law once; the commandment coming, sin revived (ἀνέζησεν), and I died (ἀπέθανον). For if sin truly is dead without law, how is it not plausible (πιθανόν) to think sin is in a way made alive (ζωοποιεῖσθαι) through the law, which also makes it manifest (ἐμφανῆ) and as it were makes it breathing (ἔμπνουν), though formerly not known (ἐγνωσμένην), even if it was in us? For we were not righteous (δίκαιοι), but sin being as dead, because perhaps (τυχόν) there was not the condemning law, we lived, having the excuse (παραίτησιν) of ignorance well-furnished (εὐάφορμον); [Rom 4:15] for where there is no law, neither transgression (παράβασις), as he says. So the commandment having come into the middle, sin as it were revived (ἀνεβίω), and death was prepared (κατηρτίσθη) and curse (ἀρά) and penalty (δίκη) of those falling under transgressions from weakness (ἀσθενείας). And what thence? Something beyond hope (ἐλπίδος ἔξω) and unexpected (ἀδοκήτων) was done in our case; for the commandment, he says, given for life, has been found, this, to death. For as the light of the sun's ray somehow harms (κατασίνεται) those who are sick (ἠῤῥωστηκότες) in sight (ὄψιν), though being by nature sweet (γλυκύ) and much-longed-for (τριπόθητον), and it is not at all itself what wrongs, but rather the being wronged by it would be thought a charge (ἔγκλημα) against the sickness (ἀῤῥωστίας) of the sufferers; in the equal way I think he says the commandment is given as pretext (πρόφασιν) to sin, and [he] deceived (ἐξηπατῆσθαι) through it, and carried down (κατακομισθῆναι) even to death. One might say otherwise also that pleasure-love (φιλήδονον) very much is wont always to fight (μάχεσθαι) the counsels (βουλαῖς) of the law; and the ways of wickedness, checked (ἀνακοπτόμενοι) by decencies (ἐπιεικείαις), lead out against [them] more stoutly (γενικώτερον, read γεννικώτερον?), and at times plunder (καταληΐζονται) the mind (νοῦν), overturning [it] into transgression, and bringing [it] under the penalties (ποιναῖς) from law, though having had (ἐσχηκότες) law as the occasion (ἀφορμήν) of war (πολέμου). Therefore Paul, being wise, says he was deceived through the commandment, and through it died; for it killed (ἀπέκτεινε), all but (μονονουχί) sharpening (καταθήγουσα) for resistance (ἀντίστασιν) the pleasures in us, according to the aforesaid ways. [Lemma Rom 7:12] So the law [is] holy (ἅγιος), and the commandment holy and just (δικαία) and good (ἀγαθή). Holy the law and the commandment holy and just and good; for it renders (ἀποφαίνει) holy and just and good those who choose to keep (φυλάττειν) it, that they might become in no way catchable (ἁλώσιμοι) by the charges (αἰτίαις) from transgressions. But this was somehow unattainable (ἀνέφικτον); [Ps 18:13 LXX] for offences (παραπτώματα) who will understand (συνήσει), according to what is written? [Lemma Rom 7:13a] Did then the good become death to me? Holy indeed the law, holy also the commandment and good. Then how did he say: And the commandment unto life was found to me, this, unto death? Tell me then, has the good become agent (πρόξενον) of ruin (ὀλέθρου)? May it not be, he says; for I accuse (ἐπαιτιῶμαι) in these things least the law, but I stand as it were accuser (κατήγορος) of sin; for it so overpowers (καταβιάζεται) the nature of man, and has mastered (κεκράτηκεν) the mind (διανοίας) in us; so that the very law [given] for salvation (σωτηρίαν) [cont. u04-rem-close].
pass_b_english: […] under sentence. Then indeed, grieving over his own carelessness and all but crying out against the strictness of the law, he will say, “I once lived apart from the law; but when the commandment came, sin came back to life, and I died” (Romans 7:9–10).

For if sin is truly dead apart from the law, is it not reasonable to think that sin is in a way brought to life through the law? For the law makes it manifest and, as it were, puts breath into it, though it was not known before, even if it was in us. For we were not righteous; but since sin was, as it were, dead, perhaps because there was no law to condemn it, we lived, and our ignorance gave us a ready plea for excuse. “For where there is no law, there is no transgression either,” as he himself says (Romans 4:15). So when the commandment came forward into the open, sin, as it were, came back to life, and death and curse and penalty were made ready for those who fall into transgressions out of weakness.

And what came of this? Something beyond all hope and expectation happened in our case. For the commandment, he says, which was given for life, was found to lead to death (Romans 7:10). Just as the light of the sun’s ray somehow harms those whose sight is sick, though by nature it is sweet and greatly longed for, and it is not the light itself at all that does the wrong, but the harm they receive from it should rather be laid to the charge of the sufferers’ sickness, so in the same way, I think, he says that the commandment gave sin an occasion, and that he was deceived through it and brought down even to death (Romans 7:11).

One might also put it another way: the love of pleasure is always very prone, in one way or another, to fight against the purposes of the law. The ways of wickedness, when they are checked by decency, march out against it the more stoutly. At times they plunder the mind, overturning it into transgression and bringing it under the penalties of the law, though it was the law that gave them the occasion for this war. This is why Paul, wise as he is, says that he was deceived through the commandment and died through it (Romans 7:11). For in effect it killed, by sharpening the pleasures within us to resist, in the ways already described.

“So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good” (Romans 7:12). The law is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good, for it makes holy and just and good those who choose to keep it, so that they may in no way be caught by the charges that arise from transgressions. But this was, in some way, beyond reach; for “who will understand his offenses?” as it is written (Psalm 19:12).

“Did that which is good, then, become death to me?” (Romans 7:13). The law is holy, and the commandment too is holy and good. How, then, did he say, “And the commandment meant for life was found, for me, to lead to death” (Romans 7:10)? Tell me, then: has the good become the bringer of ruin? “By no means,” he says (Romans 7:13). “In these words I am least of all blaming the law; I stand, as it were, as the accuser of sin. For sin so overpowers human nature and has so mastered the mind within us that the very law given to us for salvation […]

ὑπὸ δίκην· τότε δὴ τότε ταῖς ἑαυτοῦ ῥᾳθυμίαις ἐπιστυγνάσας, καὶ τῆς ἀκριβείας τοῦ
νόμου μονονουχὶ κατακεκράξεται λέγων Ἐγὼ δὲ ἔζων χωρὶς νόμου ποτέ· ἐλθούσης δὲ
τῆς ἐντολῆς ἡ ἁμαρτία ἀνέζησεν, ἐγὼ δὲ ἀπέθανον. εἰ γάρ ἐστιν ἀληθῶς ἁμαρτία νεκρὰ
χωρὶς νόμου, πῶς οὐ πιθανὸν ἐννοεῖν ζωοποιεῖσθαι τρόπον τινὰ διὰ τοῦ νόμου τὴν
ἁμαρτίαν τοῦ καὶ ἐμφανῆ καθιστάντος αὐτὴν, καὶ οἷον ἔμπνουν ἀποτελοῦντος, καίτοι
πάλαι μὴ ἐγνωσμένην, εἰ καὶ ἦν ἐν ἡμῖν; οὐ γὰρ ἦμεν δίκαιοι, ὥσπερ δὲ νεκρᾶς οὔσης
τῆς ἁμαρτίας, διά τοι τὸ μὴ εἶναι τυχὸν τὸν καταδικάζοντα νόμον, ἐζῶμεν ἡμεῖς τῆς
ἀγνοίας τὴν παραίτησιν εὐάφορμον ἔχοντες· "οὗ γὰρ οὐκ ἔστι νόμος, οὐδὲ παράβασις,"
καθά φησιν αὐτός. οὕτω παρελθούσης εἰς μέσον τῆς ἐντολῆς, ἀνεβίω μὲν ὥσπερ ἡ
ἁμαρτία, κατηρτίσθη δὲ ὁ θάνατος καὶ ἀρὰ καὶ δίκη τῶν ταῖς παραβάσεσιν
ὑποπιπτόντων ἐξ ἀσθενείας. καὶ τί τὸ ἐντεῦθεν; πέπρακταί τι τῶν ἐλπίδος ἔξω καὶ
ἀδοκήτων ἐφ' ἡμῖν· εὕρηται γὰρ ἡ ἐντολή φησιν ἡ δοθεῖσα πρὸς ζωὴν, αὕτη εἰς
θάνατον. ὥσπερ γὰρ κατασίνεταί πως τῆς ἡλιακῆς ἀκτῖνος τὸ φῶς τοὺς οἵπερ ἂν εἶεν
τὴν ὄψιν ἠῤῥωστηκότες, καίτοι πεφυκὸς εἶναι γλυκὺ καὶ τριπόθητον, καὶ οὐκ αὐτὸ
πάντως ἐστὶ τὸ ἀδικοῦν, νοοῖτο δὲ μᾶλλον τῆς τῶν πεπονθότων ἀῤῥωστίας ἔγκλημα τὸ
ἀδικεῖσθαι παρ' αὐτοῦ· κατὰ τὸν ἴσον οἶμαι τρόπον πρόφασιν διδόσθαι τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ φησὶ
τὴν ἐντολὴν, ἐξηπατῆσθαί τε δι' αὐτῆς, κατακομισθῆναι δὲ καὶ εἰς θάνατον. φαίη δ' ἄν
200 τις καὶ ἑτέρως ὅτι δὴ σφόδρα φιλεῖ ταῖς τοῦ νόμου βουλαῖς ἀεί πως μάχεσθαι τὸ
φιλήδονον· καὶ οἱ τῆς φαυλότητος τρόποι ταῖς ἐπιεικείαις ἀνακοπτόμενοι, γενικώτερον
ἀντεξάγουσι, καὶ τὸν νοῦν ἐσθ' ὅτε καταληΐζονται καταστρέφοντες εἰς παράβασιν, καὶ
ταῖς ἐκ νόμου ποιναῖς ὑποφέροντες, καίτοι νόμον ἐσχηκότες τοῦ πολέμου τὴν ἀφορμήν.

ταύτῃτοί φησι σοφὸς ὢν ὁ Παῦλος ἠπατῆσθαί τε διὰ τῆς ἐντολῆς, καὶ δι' αὐτῆς
ἀποθανεῖν· ἀπέκτεινε γὰρ μονονουχὶ καταθήγουσα πρὸς ἀντίστασιν τὰς ἐν ἡμῖν ἡδονὰς,
κατά γε τοὺς προειρημένους τρόπους. Ὥστε ὁ μὲν νόμος ἅγιος, καὶ ἡ ἐντολὴ ἁγία καὶ

ἁγίους τε καὶ δικαίους καὶ ἀγαθοὺς τοὺς οἵ περ ἂν ἕλοιντο φυλάττειν αὐτὸν, ἵνα δὴ

γέγονε θάνατος; Ἅγιος μὲν ὁ νόμος, ἁγία δὲ καὶ ἡ ἐντολὴ καὶ ἀγαθή. εἶτα πῶς ἔφασκε
"Καὶ εὑρέθη μοι ἡ ἐντολὴ ἡ εἰς ζωὴν, αὕτη εἰς "θάνατον;" ἆρα οὖν εἰπέ μοι γέγονε τὸ
ἀγαθὸν ὀλέθρου πρόξενον; μὴ γένοιτο, φησίν· ἐπαιτιῶμαι γὰρ ἐν τούτοις ἥκιστα μὲν
τὸν νόμον, ἕστηκα δὲ ὥσπερ τῆς ἁμαρτίας κατήγορος· καταβιάζεται γὰρ οὕτω τὴν
ἀνθρώπου φύσιν, καὶ τῆς ἐν ἡμῖν διανοίας κεκράτηκεν· ὥστε αὐτὸν τὸν εἰς σωτηρίαν
reviewer: claude (Wave A review, clause by clause against the Greek)
review_notes: κατηρτίσθη δὲ ὁ θάνατος καὶ ἀρὰ καὶ δίκη has three coordinate subjects; the draft made curse and penalty mere companions of death. The Romans 7:10 quotation used the archaic 'unto death'; now plain English and in line with the earlier paraphrase of the same verse. 'Given to fighting, always and in some way' was stiff word order for ἀεί πως μάχεσθαι. 'Offences' to American spelling. Psalm 19:12 (LXX 18:13) checked: correct English numbering.
Copy-text: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos via Khazarzar (Fragmenta in sancti Pauli epistulam ad Romanos.pdf).

The section opens mid-sentence (continuing πέπτωκεν | ὑπὸ δίκην from u04-rem-early) and ends mid-sentence (ὥστε αὐτὸν τὸν εἰς σωτηρίαν | ἡμῖν καὶ ζωὴν δοθέντα νόμον in u04-rem-close). Both breaks are marked […].
The page number 11 and PG column number 200 in the source block are not translated.
After 'By no means, he says', Cyril continues in Paul's first person (ἐπαιτιῶμαι, ἕστηκα); the speech is set in quotation marks to show the speaker. The quotation continues into u04-rem-close.
γενικώτερον is printed; it is read as γεννικώτερον ('more stoutly, more boldly'), which the military image (ἀντεξάγουσι, καταληΐζονται, πολέμου) requires.
ταῖς ἐπιεικείαις ('by decencies, fair restraints') is rendered 'by decency'.
In ἀπέκτεινε ... καταθήγουσα the feminine subject may be the commandment or sin; Romans 7:11 makes sin the killer. 'It' keeps the ambiguity of the Greek.
'Sweet' light (γλυκὺ ... τὸ φῶς) may echo Ecclesiastes 11:7; possible allusion only, so not cited inline.
